assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reshaped how economists and policymakers understand the labour-market effects of technology and trade. The task-based framework and the local labour-market evidence on import competition changed both research agendas and policy debate. The empirical designs are transparent and the results have been widely re-examined.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task framework and the trade-shock work. Hanson is the natural co-recipient for the China-shock evidence, with Dorn as a close collaborator. Katz is credited here but also appears in other candidates. Part of the task-approach lineage involves a researcher who has already received the prize, which complicates credit.
assessment.maturity: The work spans roughly two decades and has had time for replication, critique and extension, including debates about magnitudes and persistence. Its relevance has increased with automation and AI.
uncertainties: How to apportion credit between the task framework and the trade-shock papers
Whether the committee would prefer a narrower, single-theme prize
Ongoing debate over the size and persistence of the trade-shock effects

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Links optimal-tax theory to empirical evidence on behavioural responses, notably through the elasticity of taxable income and the sufficient-statistics approach. It has had a large, direct influence on tax policy analysis. The empirical content is well suited to scrutiny and reanalysis.
assessment.attribution: Saez is the clear intellectual leader. Slemrod is a long-standing empirical pioneer on tax avoidance and responses. Chetty and Stantcheva are important but are better placed in other candidates or are early in their careers. Feldstein's foundational contribution cannot be recognised, which narrows the set of possible recipients.
assessment.maturity: The field is mature, with decades of evidence and many natural-experiment studies. The elasticity estimates are reasonably robust across settings, though they vary.
uncertainties: Heterogeneity in elasticity estimates and sensitivity to identification choices
Overlap with the inequality candidate through Saez
Whether the committee would pair this with a theory pioneer

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification formalises what can be credibly concluded under weak assumptions. It speaks directly to the credibility of empirical claims and to the gap between assumptions and conclusions. The conceptual contribution is deep and the methods are widely applied.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the founder of the approach. Tamer is the key figure in modern moment-inequality and set-identified econometrics. Molinari is a leading contemporary contributor, but a three-person prize would dilute the founder-centred narrative.
assessment.maturity: Manski's foundational work dates from the late 1980s and 1990s, and the field has had time to develop. Applied uptake is real but narrower than for mainstream estimators.
uncertainties: Applied adoption is narrower than the conceptual importance suggests
Choice between a founder-only and a founder-plus-modern-developers prize
Competition from other econometrics candidates

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Established management practices as a measurable, causal driver of firm productivity differences through new large-scale surveys and field experiments. This links microeconomics, organisation and growth. Methodologically it combines measurement innovation with randomised evidence, which gives the results credibility.
assessment.attribution: Bloom and Van Reenen are the primary originators of the World Management Survey and the associated research programme. Sadun is an important collaborator. Bloom also appears in the uncertainty-shocks candidate, so credit is spread across several programmes.
assessment.maturity: Roughly fifteen to twenty years of work with growing replication. The field experiments in Indian textile firms are small-sample, and external validity across contexts is still being established.
uncertainties: External validity of the small-sample field experiments
Survey-based measurement of management quality and possible bias
Bloom's work is spread across two candidates

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Forms the framework through which central banks think about monetary policy, covering nominal rigidities, policy rules and the New Keynesian synthesis. Its policy influence is exceptional.
assessment.attribution: Credit is highly diffuse across at least eight listed names. Taylor (staggered contracts, rule), Calvo (pricing) and Woodford (synthesis) are the clearest of the three-person-limit options. Gertler, Gali, Christiano and Eichenbaum are strongly deserving, and any selection leaves out major contributors.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with decades of use. The framework's performance in the 2008 crisis and the post-2020 inflation episode has been debated, which is relevant to how its status is read.
uncertainties: Severe attribution problem and the three-person limit
Partial recognition of earlier rational-expectations work already honoured
Debate over the framework's empirical performance

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reframed cross-country income differences as partly a problem of resource misallocation across firms. This created a large quantitative literature in macro-development. Conceptually influential and policy-relevant.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the central paper. Restuccia and Rogerson's earlier work is a closely related and independent origin. Excluding Restuccia from a two-person selection is a credit risk.
assessment.maturity: Established since about 2008-09, with extensive follow-up. Measurement of misallocation is sensitive to the treatment of measurement error and markups.
uncertainties: Sensitivity of the misallocation estimates to measurement error and markup assumptions
Priority dispute between the Hsieh-Klenow and Restuccia-Rogerson lines
Prize narrative overlap with the growth prize awarded in 2025

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Established that fairness and reciprocity matter systematically, through experimental evidence combined with a tractable formal model (inequity aversion). It has influenced contract theory, public goods and labour economics. The experimental findings are among the better-replicated results in economics.
assessment.attribution: Fehr is the dominant figure, with the experimental programme and its theoretical interpretation. Schmidt is the co-author of the inequity-aversion model. Falk is important for field-relevant extensions. Bolton-Ockenfels is a competing model that is not on the list.
assessment.maturity: Work from the late 1990s onward, with long-run replication evidence across settings. There are debates over the stability of social preferences and how well they predict behaviour outside the lab.
uncertainties: External validity of lab-measured social preferences
Parallel model development (not credited here) complicates attribution
Behavioural economics has already been recognised several times

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Created the law-and-finance research programme, which links legal institutions to financial development and has opened a wide empirical literature on institutions. It has been highly influential.
assessment.attribution: Shleifer is the common thread in the group, and La Porta and Lopez-de-Silanes are the core empirical co-authors. Vishny is credited but his case rests mainly on other work. The prize would overlap with recognition of institutions research in 2024.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with more than two decades of follow-up. Subsequent work has questioned the legal-origins results through coding choices, endogeneity and causal interpretation, so the robustness of the headline findings is not fully settled.
uncertainties: Reproducibility and robustness of the cross-country legal-origins regressions
Overlap with the 2024 institutions prize
Causal interpretation of legal origin
Contested reputational and controversy factors
